chapters.name: Chapter 1: Plan and build your site

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How websites work, and planning your page
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a simple plan for a one-page website.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real or practice group or business, you will plan a one-page website with its audience, one action for visitors, sections and photos, with four or five sections and only photos you may use.
A website is a set of pages stored on a computer called a server. When you type an address, your browser asks that server for the page and shows it to you.
Before building, plan. Answer four questions: Who is the site for? What is the one thing visitors should do (call, visit, sign up, donate)? What sections do you need? What pictures can you use with permission?
Most small community sites need just a few sections: a title, an "About us", what you offer, hours and how to reach you.
Step by step:
- Write who the site is for.
- Write the one action you want visitors to take.
- List four or five sections.
- List photos you own or have permission to use.
Words to know:
- Website: one or more pages people can visit on the internet.
- Server: a computer that stores websites and sends pages to visitors.
- Browser: the program you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Edge or Safari.
Try it now: Choose a real or practice group (for example a youth tutoring club or a family food truck). Write your plan: who it is for, the one action, five sections and two photos you can use.
You can now explain how a website reaches you and plan a one-page site.

options: A computer that stores websites and sends pages
check.why: A server stores web pages and sends them when a browser asks.

check.q: Your food truck site should get people to come eat. What is the one action?
options: Find where and when the truck will be
check.why: The one action is what you most want visitors to do, like visit the truck.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a free site with Google Sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a Google Site with a title and your planned sections.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free Google account, you will create a Google Site with a title, a text box for each planned section and a readable theme, without help.
Google Sites is a free website builder that comes with a Google account. You build by clicking and typing, not by writing code.
Open sites.google.com on a computer and start a new site, either blank or from a template. Give the site a name and type a page title. On the right side you will find Insert (to add text boxes, images and more), Pages and Themes.
Add a text box for each section from your plan. Pick a theme with easy-to-read colors. Google Sites saves your work as you go.
Step by step:
- Go to sites.google.com and sign in with your Google account.
- Start a new site from blank or a template.
- Type the site name and page title.
- Use Insert on the right to add a text box for each section.
- Choose an easy-to-read theme.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you fill in with your own words.
- Theme: the colors and fonts used across your site.
Official sources:
- Google Sites Help: Create, name or copy a site
Try it now: Start a new Google Site for your group. Add the title and an empty text box for each section in your plan, and choose a theme.
You can now build the frame of a free website with Google Sites.

check.q: What does a theme in Google Sites change?
check.why: A theme sets the colors and fonts of your site.

check.q: You want to add an "Hours" section to your Google Site. What do you click?
check.why: Insert on the right side adds text boxes, images and more.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing your web text with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a free AI assistant to draft your About section, then make it your own.
This lesson builds toward: Given your group's real facts, you will write an About Us section with an AI assistant and edit it in your own words, removing every wrong or made-up fact.
A free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can write a first draft of your web text. Give it the facts and the tone you want.
Example prompt: "Write a friendly 60-word About Us for a free after-school tutoring club at a community center. We help kids in grades 3 to 8 with reading and math. Use simple words."
Then edit. Fix any fact the AI got wrong or made up, cut words that do not sound like you, and never let it invent prices, awards or promises you cannot keep. Your site speaks for your group, so you are responsible for every word.
Step by step:
- Give the AI your group's real facts and the tone you want.
- Ask for a short draft with a word limit.
- Fix wrong or made-up facts.
- Rewrite parts so they sound like you, then paste into your site.
Words to know:
- Draft: a first version you will improve.
- Tone: how writing sounds: friendly, serious, cheerful.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a 60-word About Us for your group. Fix one fact or phrase, then paste the edited version into your Google Site.
You can now use AI to draft web text and edit it so it is true and sounds like you.

check.q: Why give the AI a word limit for your About Us?
options: So the draft is short and fits your page
check.why: A word limit keeps the draft short enough for a small website.

check.q: The AI's draft says your tutoring is "guaranteed to raise grades". What do you do?
options: Remove the promise you cannot keep
check.why: Never let the AI add promises you cannot keep; you are responsible for every word.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Reading simple HTML
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes Goal: Read a short piece of HTML and change its words safely. This lesson builds toward: Given a short piece of HTML in an online editor, you will identify its tags and change the words between them, so the page still runs correctly. HTML is the language web pages are written in. It uses tags in angle brackets. Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag like

and a closing tag like

, with words in between. Common tags:

for a heading,

for a paragraph,

    and
  • for a bulleted list, for bold, and for a link. You can practice for free, with no account, in an online editor such as the W3Schools Tryit Editor: paste HTML on the left, click Run, and see the page on the right. Change only the words between tags at first, then run it again. Step by step: - Open a free online HTML editor. - Paste a short piece of HTML. - Click Run to see the result. - Change the words between two tags and run it again. Words to know: - HTML: the language used to write web pages. - Tag: a label in angle brackets, like

    , that tells the browser what something is. - Closing tag: the end tag with a slash, like

    . Try it now: In a free online HTML editor, type

    Our Hours

    Mondays 3 to 6 pm

    . Click Run, change the hours, and run it again. You can now read simple HTML tags and safely change the words inside them.

check.q: Which tag makes a bulleted list item?
check.why: <li> marks each item in a bulleted list, inside <ul>.

check.q:
You want to change "Mondays" to "Tuesdays" in

Mondays 3 to 6 pm

. What do you change?
options: Only the word between the tags
check.why: At first, change only the words between tags so the HTML still works.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting AI to write code, then testing and fixing it
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Ask AI for a small HTML box, test it, fix one problem and add it to your site.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will ask for a simple HTML box, test it, fix one problem and embed it in your Google Site, with every fact right and no scripts you did not ask for.
AI assistants can write HTML. Be specific: "Write simple HTML only, no JavaScript, for a box with the heading Hours and Contact, a list of our hours (Mon to Thu 3 to 6 pm), and a link to our email. Use a light background and large text."
Always test AI code before you use it. Paste it into the online editor, click Run and check: Is every fact right? Does the link work? Is the text easy to read? If something is wrong, tell the AI exactly what to fix, or fix the words yourself.
Do not paste code you do not understand from strangers or from AI that includes scripts you did not ask for. To add your box to Google Sites: click Insert, then Embed, choose Embed code, paste your HTML, click Next and Insert.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for simple HTML only, with your real hours and contact.
- Test it in the online editor.
- Fix one thing: a fact, a link or the text size.
- In Google Sites: Insert, Embed, Embed code, paste, Next, Insert.
Words to know:
- Code: instructions written for a computer, like HTML.
- Embed: to place a piece of code or content inside a page.
- Bug: a mistake in code that makes it work wrong.
Official sources:
- Google Sites Help: Embed HTML or JavaScript in your site
Try it now: Ask AI for a simple HTML Hours and Contact box for your group. Test it, fix one problem, and embed it on your Google Site.
You can now get working HTML from AI, test it, fix it and add it to a site.

check.q: Why ask the AI for "simple HTML only, no JavaScript"?
options: Simple HTML is safer and easier for a beginner to check
check.why: Simple HTML is easy to read and test, with no scripts you did not ask for.

check.q: You tested the AI's box and the email link does not work. What do you do?
options: Tell the AI exactly what to fix, or fix it yourself, then test again
Remove the email from the plan
check.why: Fix the one problem and test again before you use the code.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Publishing and checking your site
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Publish your site, check it on a phone and protect private information.
This lesson builds toward: When your site is ready, you will publish it, check it on a phone and remove private information, with working links, readable text and no private address, personal number or unapproved photos.
When your page is ready, click Publish at the top right of Google Sites. Choose a web address and publish. You can make changes later and publish again.
Check your live site on a phone, because most visitors will use one. Is the text big enough? Do the links work? Do pictures load? Ask a friend to try it too.
Protect privacy. Do not post a home address, a personal cell number or photos of children without written permission from a parent or guardian. Use a group email or a public meeting place instead.
Step by step:
- Click Publish, choose the web address, and publish.
- Open the live address on a phone.
- Check text size, links and pictures.
- Remove any private address, personal number or photo without permission.
Words to know:
- Publish: make your site live so anyone with the address can see it.
- Web address: the text you type to visit a site, also called a URL.
Try it now: Final task: publish your one-page Google Site with your edited About section and tested Hours and Contact box. Check it on a phone and remove anything private.
You can now publish a working website, check it on a phone and keep private information off it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Site built No clear title or sections missing. A Google Site with a clear title and the planned sections in a readable theme. The one action for visitors is easy to find. About Us AI text pasted as is, or with wrong or made-up facts. Short About Us with true facts, edited in the learner's own words. Can point to what they changed and why. Hours and Contact box No HTML box, or it was not tested. A simple HTML box tested in an editor, one problem fixed, and embedded. Can explain what each tag in the box does. Published and phone-ready Not published, or not checked on a phone. Published and checked on a phone: text readable, links work, pictures load. A friend also tested it and any problems were fixed. Privacy A home address, personal number or unapproved child photo is on the site. Only a group email or public place, and no private details. All photos are owned or used with written permission. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What happens when you click Publish in Google Sites?
options: The site goes live at the web address you chose
check.why: Publishing makes the site live at its web address.

check.q: Your site shows a member's personal cell number. What do you do?
options: Leave it; it helps people call
Ask visitors not to call it
Replace it with a group email and publish again
check.why: Personal numbers stay off public sites; use a group email instead.
